query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing lightweight, low‐density elements (e.g., Al or Ti) into the high‐entropy alloy design will yield an alloy with reduced overall density while retaining the superior mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties associated with HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional high‐entropy alloys based primarily on heavier transition metals (e.g., Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) that exhibit excellent comprehensive performance but have relatively high densities.
generation.intervention: Reformulate the alloy composition to partially replace heavier elements with lightweight elements such as Al or Ti to form an alloy (e.g., AlxCoCrFeNi or CoCrFeNiTi) while maintaining a single-phase solid solution structure.
generation.conditions: Processing by casting or similar solid–state synthesis, examined at room temperature and service temperatures up to the regime where phase stability is maintained (e.g., below the decomposition temperature of the single-phase FCC region).
generation.structural_mediator: The increased lattice distortion and high configurational entropy, alongside the beneficial incorporation of low-density atoms, will mediate a modified microstructural state that balances reduced mass with maintained phase integrity and defect-induced strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Lightweight elements have lower atomic weights and, when incorporated into the multi‐principal element matrix, reduce the overall alloy density. Simultaneously, the high-entropy (cocktail) effect promotes the formation of a stable single-phase structure, enhancing mechanical strength and corrosion resistance despite the density reduction.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new composition is predicted to show a moderate reduction in density (improving lightweight characteristics) while retaining or even enhancing mechanical strength, thermal stability, and corrosion resistance compared to traditional, heavier HEAs.
generation.baseline: Traditional HEAs such as CrMnFeCoNi with heavier constituent elements and no intentional incorporation of low-density elements.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected as long as the introduced lightweight elements do not significantly destabilize the single-phase solid solution or form brittle intermetallics; performance may degrade if phase decomposition or embrittlement occurs at elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of weight reduction and its trade-offs with properties such as hardness and yield strength remain uncertain and require experimental optimization, especially under long-term high-temperature exposure.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA samples: one set with a traditional heavy composition (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) and a second set with a partial replacement by lightweight elements (e.g., Al or Ti additions to form AlxCoCrFeNi or CoCrFeNiTi). Process the samples under identical casting and annealing conditions to ensure a single-phase structure.
measurements: Density (using Archimedes method or similar) to quantify weight reduction.
Mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, ductility) at room and elevated temperatures.
Phase analysis through X-ray diffraction (XRD) to verify the stability of the single-phase structure.
Corrosion resistance tests under relevant environmental conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the lightweight-element-containing HEA does not show a statistically significant reduction in density without concurrent degradation (or if it shows deterioration) in mechanical or thermal performance compared to the baseline traditional HEA, then the hypothesis that incorporation of lightweight elements enables superior comprehensive performance with a reduced density is falsified.

The comprehensive effect of the mixing of various main elements endows the high entropy alloy with high entropy effect in thermodynamics, lattice distortion effect in structure, hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, and “cocktail” effect in performance [ [1] , [2] ]. High–entropy alloys (HEAs) have had remarkable progress and advancement since their development by Professor Yeh in 2004. The term “high–entropy alloy” generally refers to a single–phase solid solution alloy with a simple crystal structure composed of five or more elements, with an atomic percentage ranging from 5% to 35% [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. Given their superior hardness, exceptional strength, resistance to corrosion, and a multitude of additional benefits, HEAs have became a new type of alloy material that has received a great deal of attention in the research field during recent years and the hot point of many researches [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. The high–entropy alloy composed of five elements–Cobalt (Co), Chromium (Cr), Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), and Titanium (Ti)–in equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions exhibited a simple solid solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability. However, it suffered from a relatively low hardness and strength [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. The existing research lacked a comprehensive and thorough understanding of the microstructure and deformation dynamics of the CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
